what.text: Yohimbine is a compound in the bark of yohimbe (Pausinystalia yohimbe), an evergreen tree from central and western Africa. The bark has long been used as an aphrodisiac.

src.label: NCCIH (NIH), Yohimbe: usefulness and safety

what.text: Yohimbine blocks alpha-adrenergic receptors, part of the nervous system that controls blood vessels and arousal. That is the basis for its study in erectile dysfunction (ED).

src.label: Morales A, et al. J Urol 1987

what.text: Two kinds of product exist. Yohimbine hydrochloride tablets were once sold as a prescription drug, for example as Yocon. Yohimbe bark extracts are sold as dietary supplements. NIH says supplements may not act like the prescription drug, and the amount of yohimbine in them varies widely.

what.text: There is no FDA-approved yohimbine product in Drugs@FDA, and it is illegal in the US to sell an over-the-counter yohimbine product for ED without FDA approval.

research.text: The ED trials of yohimbine are small and old: placebo-controlled studies of 22 to 100 men, mostly from 1987 to 1998, using yohimbine hydrochloride tablets. Results were mixed. Two meta-analyses (1998 and 2021) pooled them. No trial of yohimbe supplements for ED was found.

research.title: Men with physically caused ED, 1987

facts.v: randomized, placebo-controlled, partial crossover
100 men with ED from a physical cause
yohimbine 18 mg a day or placebo
men’s reported response

research.found: 42.6% responded on yohimbine and 27.6% on placebo; the difference was not statistically significant. The authors called the response “at best marginal.”

src.label: Morales A, et al. J Urol 1987

research.title: Men with psychogenic ED, 1987

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled, partial crossover
48 men with ED of psychological cause
10 weeks; yohimbine 18 mg a day
reported improvement in sexual function

research.found: After the first phase, 62% on yohimbine and 16% on placebo reported some improvement.

src.label: Reid K, et al. Lancet 1987

research.title: Men with ED of no clear cause, 1997

facts.v: double-blind, placebo-controlled
86 men with ED without a clear physical or psychological cause
8 weeks; 30 mg a day
reported desire, satisfaction and erections; rigidity during sleep in a sleep lab

research.found: 71% responded on yohimbine and 45% on placebo. Most side effects were mild, and there were no serious adverse events.

src.label: Vogt HJ, et al. Int J Impot Res 1997

research.title: High dose in physically caused ED, 1998

facts.v: placebo-controlled; 30 days each of placebo and yohimbine
22 men with ED from a physical cause, mean age 58
100 mg yohimbine once a day
erection response by questionnaire

research.found: There was no significant difference from placebo. Anxiety, faster heart rate, more urination and headache were the most common side effects.

src.label: Telöken C, et al. J Urol 1998

research.title: Pooled analysis of 7 trials, 1998

facts.v: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized, placebo-controlled trials of yohimbine alone
7 trials
response compared with placebo; side effects

research.found: Yohimbine was more likely than placebo to produce a response (odds ratio 3.85). Serious side effects were reported as infrequent and reversible. All of these trials came before PDE5 drugs such as Viagra were approved.

src.label: Ernst E, Pittler MH. J Urol 1998 (meta-analysis)

research.title: Pooled analysis of 8 trials, 2021

facts.v: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials against placebo or no treatment
8 trials, some testing yohimbine combined with other supplements
erectile function; overall sexual function

research.found: Yohimbine alone improved erectile function more often than placebo (odds ratio 2.08) but did not significantly change overall sexual function.

src.label: Wibowo DNSA, et al. Turk J Urol 2021 (meta-analysis)

us.text: Yohimbine is not an FDA-approved drug: Drugs@FDA has no yohimbine product. Yohimbe bark is sold as a dietary supplement, which FDA does not approve or review for safety or effectiveness before sale. Since 1990, FDA rules say no over-the-counter ingredient, yohimbine named among them, may be sold as an aphrodisiac without an approved new drug application. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: none found. A search of Drugs@FDA data for yohimbine hydrochloride finds no matches. Prescription yohimbine products have been sold in the US (a California poison-centre review counted cases involving them), and Yocon tablets were listed in Canada. We found no FDA approval record for any of them.

items.text: 21 CFR 310.528 names yohimbine, yohimbine hydrochloride and yohimbinum as ingredients once sold in OTC aphrodisiacs. FDA found no adequate data that any such ingredient is safe and effective for that use, and says claims that a product arouses desire or improves sexual performance are “false, misleading, or unsupported.” Such a product is a new drug that needs FDA approval.

world.lead: Yohimbine is a prescription-only substance in Australia, and the UK’s MHRA says products containing it would normally be controlled as prescription-only medicines. Canada once listed prescription yohimbine tablets, including Yocon, but all have been cancelled. In the US, yohimbe bark is sold as a dietary supplement.

after.text: Yohimbine is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List, the 2027 List, or the 2027 Monitoring Program, and it is not in a listed class such as the S6 stimulants. Class S0 covers drugs with no current approval by any government health authority; we did not confirm whether any country approves yohimbine today. WADA has not published a ruling on it.

side.text: NIH says yohimbine has been linked to irregular heartbeat, blood pressure problems, heart attacks and seizures. Poison-centre reports describe fast heart rate, stomach upset, anxiety and high blood pressure. Dietary supplements are not reviewed by FDA before sale.

items.text: irregular heartbeat, blood pressure problems, heart attacks and seizures have been associated with yohimbine.

src.label: NCCIH (NIH), Yohimbe: usefulness and safety

items.text: 238 symptomatic adult cases reported to the California Poison Control System from 2000 to 2006; 98.7% involved supplements. Common problems were stomach upset (46%), fast heart rate (43%), anxiety or agitation (33%) and high blood pressure (25%). Outcomes were more often severe than for the average exposure.
